bibl.title: Late maturation of backward masking in auditory cortex

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: the cortical basis of auditory backward masking, and whether its unusually long maturation in children is visible in cortical responses
span.quote: Speech perception relies on the accurate resolution of brief, successive sounds that change rapidly over time. Deficits in the perception of such sounds, indicated by a reduced ability to detect signals during auditory backward masking, strongly relate to language processing difficulties in children. Backward masking during normal development has a longer maturational trajectory than many other auditory percepts, implicating the involvement of central auditory neural mechanisms with protracted developmental time courses. Despite the importance of this percept, its neural correlates are not well described at any developmental stage.

span.label: whether standard onset-responsive cortical neurons show backward masking at all, and whether juveniles show more of it than adults
span.quote: This study is the first to assess whether backward masking of tone detection occurs at the level of primary auditory cortex for standard, onset-responsive neurons, how it manifests, and whether it mirrors the prolonged development seen in children. Backward masking is the neural “detection” of a masked signal compared with the masker alone, in contrast to signal detection compared with silence. We showed that the majority of ACx neurons displayed increased thresholds for tone detection in the presence of a subsequent masker. This was the case with the use of a narrow ToneWin that measured backward masking by minimizing contamination from the noise-evoked response, as well as a longer TrialWin that intentionally included the noise-evoked response, as a potential contributor to perceptual backward masking. This “masking” correlated with both suppression of tone-evoked firing by the masker and with the reduced dynamic range of the tone detection function in the presence of a masker. This indicates that both a reduction of signal response and a higher comparative baseline contribute to auditory backward masking.

span.label: backward masking is present in ordinary cortical neurons, arises from both suppressed tone firing and a reduced dynamic range, and is larger in juveniles - mainly through the suppression
span.quote: In this study we have demonstrated that the onset responses of ACx neurons to short tones were clearly modulated by a subsequent masker. Neurometric thresholds shifted to higher tone levels in the presence of this masker. The higher thresholds seen during masking were attributable to a combination of suppressed firing to the tone and a smaller dynamic range available for detection during masking. In a developmental comparison, juvenile neurons showed both greater tone firing suppression and larger threshold shifts than adult neurons, at both single-cell and population levels. Our results are consistent with the human literature of higher backward masked thresholds extending into adolescence and demonstrate robust backward masking at the level of ACx.

span.label: mechanism
span.quote: Cortical masking was driven by a combination of suppressed responses to the signal and a reduced dynamic range available for signal detection in the presence of the masker.

span.label: auditory backward masking
span.quote: Perceptually, auditory backward masking manifests as higher thresholds for detection of a short signal followed by a masker than for the same signal in silence.

span.label: electrophysiology
span.quote: We thus recorded firing responses from auditory cortex (ACx) in response to masked and unmasked sounds in juveniles compared with adults.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Inhibition evoked by the masker arrives with a shorter latency than excitation, so it can reach back and suppress the response to the tone that preceded it.
span.quote: Backward masking was attributable to fast inhibition, where a shorter latency for inhibition compared with excitation allowed inhibition evoked by the delayed masker to suppress the response to the earlier tone.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: In immature cortex the inhibitory response to the masker is larger and slower to decay, so it truncates more of the preceding excitatory tone response and amplifies firing-rate suppression in juveniles.
span.quote: Thus a larger inhibitory response to the subsequent masker might differentially truncate a previous excitatory response to the tone in young neurons, magnifying tone-evoked firing rate suppression.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Juveniles integrate over a longer listening window, which pulls more masker-driven firing into the comparison baseline, shrinking the dynamic range and raising masked thresholds.
span.quote: If juveniles integrate over a longer window than adults, they would experience larger dynamic range differences due to incorporating more firing activity from the masker.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Unrefined inhibition in cortex or in presynaptic regions lets an off-frequency noise masker suppress juvenile responses more than adult ones.
span.quote: In juveniles, the differentially increased suppression in the presence of a noise masker that activates off-frequency neurons may be due to unrefined inhibition in cortex or in presynaptic regions.

span.label: masking arises from a reduction of the signal response together with a higher comparative baseline, which narrows the dynamic range available for detection
span.quote: This study is the first to assess whether backward masking of tone detection occurs at the level of primary auditory cortex for standard, onset-responsive neurons, how it manifests, and whether it mirrors the prolonged development seen in children. Backward masking is the neural “detection” of a masked signal compared with the masker alone, in contrast to signal detection compared with silence. We showed that the majority of ACx neurons displayed increased thresholds for tone detection in the presence of a subsequent masker. This was the case with the use of a narrow ToneWin that measured backward masking by minimizing contamination from the noise-evoked response, as well as a longer TrialWin that intentionally included the noise-evoked response, as a potential contributor to perceptual backward masking. This “masking” correlated with both suppression of tone-evoked firing by the masker and with the reduced dynamic range of the tone detection function in the presence of a masker. This indicates that both a reduction of signal response and a higher comparative baseline contribute to auditory backward masking.

span.label: and a shorter latency for inhibition than for excitation lets the later masker suppress the earlier tone, which also explains why a suppressed masker response masks less
span.quote: Mechanistically, forward masking is considered to involve a combination of synaptic depression, afterhyperpolarization, and inhibition ( Brosch and Schreiner 1997 ; Wehr and Zador 2005 ). A study of forward and backward masking in the bat inferior colliculus indicates that mechanisms involving the relative timing of inhibition and excitation at the level of the inferior colliculus can explain both types of masking ( Faure et al. 2003 ). Backward masking was attributable to fast inhibition, where a shorter latency for inhibition compared with excitation allowed inhibition evoked by the delayed masker to suppress the response to the earlier tone. Such a mechanism could explain the negative correlation seen in the present study between forward masking of the noise with backward masking of the tone in the narrow ToneWin: a suppressed response to the masker would be less effective at suppressing the tone response.

span.label: so the cortical effect may be inherited from earlier regions, with cortex possibly adding to it by reducing rebound excitation
span.quote: Cortical masked responses, expressed as a reduction in tone-evoked firing, may thus be inherited from earlier brain regions. It remains possible that cortex further increases masking. In gerbil ACx, both tone-evoked afterhyperpolarizations and rebound firing were reduced in magnitude by a temporally overlapping masker ( Gay et al. 2014 ). Backward masking may induce a similar reduction of rebound excitation, which would magnify the suppression of tone-evoked firing at the level of cortex.

span.label: and the immature version is attributed to inhibition that decays more slowly and summates more in young neurons
span.quote: An additional challenge to juvenile signal detection with backward maskers is the greater tone-evoked firing suppression shown in the present study. In addition to inefficient temporal integration, this differential signal suppression could contribute to the large age-related threshold differences seen in psychophysical backward masking (~25-dB differences around age 9, and still ~10-dB differences by age 15; Huyck and Wright 2018 ; Wright and Zecker 2004 ). Although the basis for backward masking is poorly understood, its gradual maturation implies that neural mechanisms with long developmental time courses may be involved ( Rosen et al. 2010 ). Inhibition in the central auditory system is known to have a long developmental trajectory ( Chang et al. 2005 ; Gao et al. 1999 ; Sun et al. 2010 ) and to sculpt responses to time-varying percepts such as frequency modulation discrimination, forward masking, and duration tuning ( Razak and Fuzessery 2007 ; 2009 ; Sayegh et al. 2014 ; Volkov and Galazyuk 1992 ; Zhang et al. 2003 ). Tone-evoked suppression via masking likely involves inhibitory circuitry. In juveniles, the differentially increased suppression in the presence of a noise masker that activates off-frequency neurons may be due to unrefined inhibition in cortex or in presynaptic regions. Immature on-frequency inhibition may also contribute. In cortical pyramidal neurons, the decay time constants for inhibition are much slower during development than in adulthood ( Cai et al. 2017 ; Takesian et al. 2012 ). Closely spaced stimuli led to greater overlap and summation of inhibition in young neurons when tested in vivo ( Cai et al. 2017 ). Thus a larger inhibitory response to the subsequent masker might differentially truncate a previous excitatory response to the tone in young neurons, magnifying tone-evoked firing rate suppression. In contrast to firing rate suppression, the masker-induced reduction in dynamic range only differs across age for the narrow ToneWin. The firing suppression may thus be a particular driver of increased backward masked thresholds in Juveniles. Overall, the slow maturation of backward masking may be influenced by the gradual development of inhibition throughout the auditory pathway.

span.label: Recordings were made under anesthesia, which complicates extrapolation to psychophysics.
span.quote: Anesthesia is one concern in extending our neural responses to psychophysical comparisons.

span.label: It is unknown whether the nervous system actually reads out only the narrow tone-response window the analysis assumes.
span.quote: Although the ToneWin measures backward masking of the tone, it is unknown whether the nervous system is analyzing activity only within this window to decide whether a tone is present.

span.label: The population neurometric pools every recorded cell, which is both its strength and its weakness.
span.quote: A strength and limitation of the population neurometric used in the present study is that it pools information across all cells to make a decision for or against tone detection.

span.label: Including non-responsive neurons should degrade the pooled neurometric, and whether that degradation is age-dependent is unknown.
span.quote: Thus the performance of the pooling neurometric on masked tone detection should be reduced by incorporating responses from nonresponsive neurons, but whether this effect would vary across age is unknown.

span.label: Single units and multiunits were pooled because multiunits dominated the dataset.
span.quote: Because MUs dominated the data set, all SUs and MUs were pooled for analysis.

span.label: it is unknown whether the nervous system analyses only the narrow window, and finding out would require trial-by-trial mapping of activity onto behavioral choice
span.quote: Although the ToneWin measures backward masking of the tone, it is unknown whether the nervous system is analyzing activity only within this window to decide whether a tone is present. Understanding the relationship between individual neurons’ activity and perceptual judgment requires the choosing of an analysis window that mimics the decision window used by the listener. However, this window is typically variable and difficult to determine ( Nienborg et al. 2012 ). Understanding the relevant time windows that contribute to perception requires trial-by-trial mapping of neural activity with behavioral choice

span.label: the population neurometric pools every cell, which is both its strength and its limitation, and sits against the rival principle that only the most sensitive neurons matter
span.quote: A strength and limitation of the population neurometric used in the present study is that it pools information across all cells to make a decision for or against tone detection. In general, population coding assumes that all active neurons contribute to perception, whereas the lower envelope principle assumes that perception is driven by the most sensitive neurons and that less sensitive neurons will not interfere

span.label: and because every neuron was tested at its own best frequency, the pooled measure is optimistic in a way the paper spells out
span.quote: Because all neurons in this study were presented with stimuli at BF, our neurometric does not reflect the situation where a downstream integrator neuron would also receive input from cells that were poorly tuned to the stimulus. In studies where neurons were explicitly tested with preferred and nonpreferred stimuli, pooling of all active neurons regardless of their stimulus specificity reduced the performance of the neurometric, effectively raising detection thresholds ( Purushothaman and Bradley 2005 ). This effect held true for neurons in ACx, where neural performance for song discrimination in songbirds ( Wang et al. 2007 ) and for encoding amplitude modulation depth in gerbils ( Rosen et al. 2010 ) only achieved accuracy as good as behavior when only the best neurons were included. Thus the performance of the pooling neurometric on masked tone detection should be reduced by incorporating responses from nonresponsive neurons, but whether this effect would vary across age is unknown.

span.label: anesthesia is named as a concern for the comparison with psychophysics, with urethane chosen to keep the cortex closest to the awake state
span.quote: Anesthesia is one concern in extending our neural responses to psychophysical comparisons. We used anesthesia to maximize data collection during extended masking protocols; we chose urethane to minimize anesthetic effects. Ketamine primarily affects NMDA receptors, and pentobarbital enhances GABA A receptor effects. Under these drugs, the cortex operates mostly in the synchronized state. In contrast, urethane anesthesia is produced by a modest effect on multiple receptor systems ( Hara and Harris 2002 ) and allows desynchronized activity to occur spontaneously in cortex, more similar to the awake state ( Curto et al. 2009 ). In the avian analog of ACx, urethane decreases both spontaneous and evoked activity ( Capsius and Leppelsack 1996 ). Because the relationship between spontaneous and driven activity drives the neural detection measures, urethane potentially minimizes any deviation from awake recordings. Qualitatively, both juvenile and adult recordings resembled those from awake, restrained gerbils ( Rosen et al. 2010 ), although restraint is known to affect cortical responses, as well

span.label: and the authors' own earlier null on the best neurons suggests the difference may lie in how the information is used rather than in how it is encoded
span.quote: In a previous study, we observed no age difference in the thresholds of the best neurons in gerbil ACx tuned to modulation detection, suggesting that juvenile and adult animals may not equivalently access the sensory information in these most sensitive neurons ( Rosen et al. 2010 ). Differential use of sensory information could amplify the age differences visible with the use of the cell-by-cell and population analyses applied in the present study, but this would need to be assessed by recording in decision-making regions during task performance.

span.label: The two-alternative forced-choice detection procedure and threshold-shift logic of human masking experiments is carried over to single-unit spike counts as a neurometric, so that neural thresholds can be compared directly with psychometric ones.
span.quote: We presented our stimuli and analyzed our data with methods analogous to those used during behavioral detection experiments to best understand the neural responses that could underlie the perceptual phenomenon.

span.label: the masked-versus-unmasked threshold comparison, reproduced in the neurometric so the two can be put side by side
span.quote: Our neurometric comparison used Noise-Alone-evoked firing and spontaneous firing as the backgrounds against which each threshold was determined to match perceptual measures. In psychophysical detection, listeners choose between alternatives of a masker with and without a tone, to yield a masked detection threshold. A separate choice between silence and a tone yields a Tone-Alone detection threshold. The two thresholds are then compared to yield a mask-induced threshold shift. Because the masker immediately follows the tone, a longer detection window such as the TrialWin will encompass the response to the masker, making the relative background level a critical element of detection above baseline. In contrast, only a very short analysis window will exclude the Noise-Alone-evoked firing background.

span.label: the encoding time window as an explicit parameter, and the requirement to choose one
span.quote: Neurometric analysis requires the choosing of an appropriate encoding time window, defined as the window containing the response patterns contributing to the signal to be detected ( Panzeri et al. 2010 ). For these neurometric analyses, we employed two windows to test different aspects of masking. First, a brief analysis window encompassed only the response to the tone without any response to the successive masker. This quantified backward masking of the tone response while excluding forward masking of the subsequent masker response by the tone, allowing a measure of cortical backward masking uncontaminated by a forward masked component. Second, a longer analysis window encompassed the response to both the tone and the subsequent masker. This was used because behaviorally, tone detection in the presence of a masker is measured in comparison to that of the masker alone, and because the behavioral reaction time for short signal detection occurs well after subsequent masker onset. Thus perception of backward masked signals could be influenced by neural responses to the masker, which are encompassed by the longer analysis window. The longer window may more accurately reflect the information used by the nervous system for masked signal detection.

span.label: population coding, which assumes that all active neurons contribute to perception, against the lower envelope principle, which assumes that perception is driven by the most sensitive neurons
span.quote: A strength and limitation of the population neurometric used in the present study is that it pools information across all cells to make a decision for or against tone detection. In general, population coding assumes that all active neurons contribute to perception, whereas the lower envelope principle assumes that perception is driven by the most sensitive neurons and that less sensitive neurons will not interfere

span.label: the relative-timing-of-inhibition account of masking
span.quote: Mechanistically, forward masking is considered to involve a combination of synaptic depression, afterhyperpolarization, and inhibition ( Brosch and Schreiner 1997 ; Wehr and Zador 2005 ). A study of forward and backward masking in the bat inferior colliculus indicates that mechanisms involving the relative timing of inhibition and excitation at the level of the inferior colliculus can explain both types of masking ( Faure et al. 2003 ). Backward masking was attributable to fast inhibition, where a shorter latency for inhibition compared with excitation allowed inhibition evoked by the delayed masker to suppress the response to the earlier tone. Such a mechanism could explain the negative correlation seen in the present study between forward masking of the noise with backward masking of the tone in the narrow ToneWin: a suppressed response to the masker would be less effective at suppressing the tone response.

span.label: a SECOND analysis window spanning the entire trial, beside the assumption-bearing one
span.quote: To avoid this assumption, we chose a second time window that spanned the entire trial.

span.label: masker
span.quote: Perceptually, auditory backward masking manifests as higher thresholds for detection of a short signal followed by a masker than for the same signal in silence. Cortical masking was driven by a combination of suppressed responses to the signal and a reduced dynamic range available for signal detection in the presence of the masker. Both coding elements contributed to greater masked threshold shifts in juveniles compared with adults, but signal-evoked firing suppression was more pronounced in juveniles. Neural threshold shifts were a better match to human psychophysical threshold shifts when quantified with a longer temporal window that included the response to the delayed masker, suggesting that temporally selective listening may contribute to age-related differences in backward masking.

span.label: threshold
span.quote: Perceptually, auditory backward masking manifests as higher thresholds for detection of a short signal followed by a masker than for the same signal in silence. Cortical masking was driven by a combination of suppressed responses to the signal and a reduced dynamic range available for signal detection in the presence of the masker. Both coding elements contributed to greater masked threshold shifts in juveniles compared with adults, but signal-evoked firing suppression was more pronounced in juveniles. Neural threshold shifts were a better match to human psychophysical threshold shifts when quantified with a longer temporal window that included the response to the delayed masker, suggesting that temporally selective listening may contribute to age-related differences in backward masking.

span.label: dynamic range
span.quote: With this characterization, we then asked whether the extended human maturational trajectory for backward masking is reflected in ACx responses, as would be expected based on cortical involvement in conscious masked signal detection ( Wiegand and Gutschalk 2012 ). Tone threshold shifts were larger in juveniles than in adults, indicating greater cortical backward masking. This was accompanied by a larger suppression of tone-evoked firing in juveniles, but no age-related difference in dynamic range reduction, indicating that greater juvenile masking in cortex was driven more by suppressed tone-evoked firing than by increased noise-evoked baseline. However, dynamic range reduction measured in the narrow ToneWin correlated with masked tone threshold shift only in juveniles, suggesting that dynamic range may contribute more to signal detection in juveniles than in adults.

span.label: juvenile
span.quote: With this characterization, we then asked whether the extended human maturational trajectory for backward masking is reflected in ACx responses, as would be expected based on cortical involvement in conscious masked signal detection ( Wiegand and Gutschalk 2012 ). Tone threshold shifts were larger in juveniles than in adults, indicating greater cortical backward masking. This was accompanied by a larger suppression of tone-evoked firing in juveniles, but no age-related difference in dynamic range reduction, indicating that greater juvenile masking in cortex was driven more by suppressed tone-evoked firing than by increased noise-evoked baseline. However, dynamic range reduction measured in the narrow ToneWin correlated with masked tone threshold shift only in juveniles, suggesting that dynamic range may contribute more to signal detection in juveniles than in adults.

span.label: MUs → analysis
span.note: AN ANALYST DECISION WITH ITS REASON GIVEN: because multiunits dominated the data set, all single units and multiunits were POOLED for analysis. The composition is 15 SU / 27 MU in adults and 10 SU / 30 MU in juveniles, so the pooling decision is load-bearing for every comparison that follows. No edge type records a choice the analysts made.
span.quote: Spikes were detected offline (Plexon Offline Sorter, Dallas TX), and sorted into single (SU) or multiunits (MU) on the basis of spike shape and principal component analysis. Adult neurons ( n = 42) consisted of 15 SUs and 27 MUs, whereas juvenile neurons ( n = 40) consisted of 10 SUs and 30 MUs. Because MUs dominated the data set, all SUs and MUs were pooled for analysis.

span.label: THE ANALYSIS WINDOW IS A CHOICE, AND THE REASONS ARE GIVEN BEFORE THE RESULT: a brief window isolates backward masking uncontaminated by forward masking, a longer one includes the masker response because behavioral reaction times fall well after masker onset
span.quote: Neurometric analysis requires the choosing of an appropriate encoding time window, defined as the window containing the response patterns contributing to the signal to be detected ( Panzeri et al. 2010 ). For these neurometric analyses, we employed two windows to test different aspects of masking. First, a brief analysis window encompassed only the response to the tone without any response to the successive masker. This quantified backward masking of the tone response while excluding forward masking of the subsequent masker response by the tone, allowing a measure of cortical backward masking uncontaminated by a forward masked component. Second, a longer analysis window encompassed the response to both the tone and the subsequent masker. This was used because behaviorally, tone detection in the presence of a masker is measured in comparison to that of the masker alone, and because the behavioral reaction time for short signal detection occurs well after subsequent masker onset. Thus perception of backward masked signals could be influenced by neural responses to the masker, which are encompassed by the longer analysis window. The longer window may more accurately reflect the information used by the nervous system for masked signal detection.

span.label: AND THE TWO WINDOWS GIVE DIFFERENT NUMBERS: about 18 to 43 dB of threshold shift in the longer window against 13 to 16 dB in the narrow one, with human psychophysics at 20 to 35 dB
span.quote: Consistent with this idea, the TrialWin population neurometric threshold shifts (~18–43 dB in adults) are a better match to psychometric backward masking thresholds than the ToneWin shifts (~13–16 dB in adults). In humans, masking parameters similar to those used here yield threshold shifts of ~20–35 dB ( Elliott 1962 ; Pickett 1959 ). Indeed, more units exhibited higher threshold shifts with the use of the TrialWin than the ToneWin, and this was reflected in the population neurometrics. Perception of masked signals may thus rely on longer time windows, where the neural response to the masker would increase backward masked detection thresholds.

span.label: THE CORRECT WINDOW CANNOT BE DETERMINED FROM THIS DATA: it would require trial-by-trial mapping of neural activity onto behavioral choice, and IN LIEU OF SUCH DATA the longer window is chosen for two stated reasons
span.quote: Although the ToneWin measures backward masking of the tone, it is unknown whether the nervous system is analyzing activity only within this window to decide whether a tone is present. Understanding the relationship between individual neurons’ activity and perceptual judgment requires the choosing of an analysis window that mimics the decision window used by the listener. However, this window is typically variable and difficult to determine ( Nienborg et al. 2012 ). Understanding the relevant time windows that contribute to perception requires trial-by-trial mapping of neural activity with behavioral choice

span.label: with both reasons named - detection is measured against the masker alone, and the behavioral reaction time falls well after the masker begins
span.quote: In lieu of such data, we chose the TrialWin to encompass the response to both the tone and the masker for two reasons: 1 ) perceptually, tone detection in the presence of a masker is measured in comparison to the masker alone, and the masker response occurs immediately following or even overlapping the preceding tone response; and 2 ) the behavioral reaction time for short signal detection occurs well after subsequent masker onset, suggesting that neural responses to the masker may contribute to masked signal detection.

span.label: A STRENGTH AND A LIMITATION IN ONE SENTENCE: the population neurometric pools every cell, which sits against the rival principle that perception is driven by the most sensitive neurons alone
span.quote: A strength and limitation of the population neurometric used in the present study is that it pools information across all cells to make a decision for or against tone detection. In general, population coding assumes that all active neurons contribute to perception, whereas the lower envelope principle assumes that perception is driven by the most sensitive neurons and that less sensitive neurons will not interfere

span.label: AND THE DIRECTION OF THE OWN BIAS IS SPELLED OUT: because every neuron was tested at its own best frequency, the pooled measure omits the poorly tuned cells a real integrator would receive, and would perform worse if they were included
span.quote: Because all neurons in this study were presented with stimuli at BF, our neurometric does not reflect the situation where a downstream integrator neuron would also receive input from cells that were poorly tuned to the stimulus. In studies where neurons were explicitly tested with preferred and nonpreferred stimuli, pooling of all active neurons regardless of their stimulus specificity reduced the performance of the neurometric, effectively raising detection thresholds ( Purushothaman and Bradley 2005 ). This effect held true for neurons in ACx, where neural performance for song discrimination in songbirds ( Wang et al. 2007 ) and for encoding amplitude modulation depth in gerbils ( Rosen et al. 2010 ) only achieved accuracy as good as behavior when only the best neurons were included. Thus the performance of the pooling neurometric on masked tone detection should be reduced by incorporating responses from nonresponsive neurons, but whether this effect would vary across age is unknown.

span.label: THE VARIABILITY IS ITSELF A POINT OF CORRESPONDENCE: masked thresholds are quite variable IN CONCURRENCE WITH the psychophysical data, where more measures per participant are needed than for forward masking
span.quote: First, masked thresholds are quite variable, in concurrence with psychophysical data: behaviorally, backward masking thresholds are highly variable, both within and across subjects; more threshold measures need to be gathered per participant than in forward masking to yield clear data ( Hartley et al. 2000 ; Oxenham and Moore 1995 ; also Huyck JJ, personal communication). Similarly, there was not a highly systematic relationship in our ACx data between masker level and threshold shifts, unlike the tight correlation seen with cortical and psychophysical forward masking

span.label: A CORRELATE THAT IS NOT THE CAUSE, SAID PLAINLY: masking correlated with tone-evoked suppression but could occur in its absence, and thus was not the sole driver
span.quote: A response to the masker was not required to produce masking, as also seen in cortical forward masking ( Calford and Semple 1995 ). Backward masking was correlated with tone-evoked firing suppression but could occur in its absence, and thus was not the sole driver of the masking.

span.label: THE METHOD IS ALIGNED TO THE LITERATURE IT WILL BE COMPARED WITH: stimuli were delivered monaurally to parallel the majority of psychophysical backward masking studies
span.quote: Stimuli were delivered monaurally to the right ear through an in-ear headphone speaker (Audio Technica ATH-CKS1100iS). This was chosen to parallel the majority of psychophysical backward masking studies that present stimuli monaurally.

span.label: and the inclusion rule is set by the perceptual phenomenon rather than by the recording - only units responding reliably to short tones, because backward masking is reliable only for short tones
span.quote: Neurons were isolated based on their reliable, short-latency onset responses to a 200-ms tone pip used as a search stimulus. Offset-responsive neurons were rarely encountered and were not used in these analyses. The best frequency (BF) of the unit was determined with an iso-intensity function at 60 dB SPL. For the remaining data collection, neurons were presented with short tone pips (10 ms; 2-ms cosine-ramped rise/fall) at the BF of the unit, and only units that responded reliably to these short-duration tones were recorded (firing above baseline on at least 50% of trials within 50 ms of tone onset). This is because, perceptually, the phenomena of backward masking is reliable only for short-duration tones.

span.label: A POOLING DECISION JUSTIFIED BY THE COMPOSITION OF THE SAMPLE: single and multi-units were pooled BECAUSE multi-units dominated the data set
span.quote: Spikes were detected offline (Plexon Offline Sorter, Dallas TX), and sorted into single (SU) or multiunits (MU) on the basis of spike shape and principal component analysis. Adult neurons ( n = 42) consisted of 15 SUs and 27 MUs, whereas juvenile neurons ( n = 40) consisted of 10 SUs and 30 MUs. Because MUs dominated the data set, all SUs and MUs were pooled for analysis.

span.label: THE anesthetic IS JUSTIFIED BY MECHANISM RATHER THAN WAVED AWAY: urethane acts modestly on multiple receptor systems and allows desynchronised cortical activity, unlike ketamine or pentobarbital
span.quote: Anesthesia is one concern in extending our neural responses to psychophysical comparisons. We used anesthesia to maximize data collection during extended masking protocols; we chose urethane to minimize anesthetic effects. Ketamine primarily affects NMDA receptors, and pentobarbital enhances GABA A receptor effects. Under these drugs, the cortex operates mostly in the synchronized state. In contrast, urethane anesthesia is produced by a modest effect on multiple receptor systems ( Hara and Harris 2002 ) and allows desynchronized activity to occur spontaneously in cortex, more similar to the awake state ( Curto et al. 2009 ). In the avian analog of ACx, urethane decreases both spontaneous and evoked activity ( Capsius and Leppelsack 1996 ). Because the relationship between spontaneous and driven activity drives the neural detection measures, urethane potentially minimizes any deviation from awake recordings. Qualitatively, both juvenile and adult recordings resembled those from awake, restrained gerbils ( Rosen et al. 2010 ), although restraint is known to affect cortical responses, as well

span.label: AND THE AUTHORS' OWN EARLIER NULL COMPLICATES THE STORY: no age difference in the thresholds of the BEST neurons, suggesting juveniles and adults may not equivalently ACCESS the same sensory information
span.quote: In a previous study, we observed no age difference in the thresholds of the best neurons in gerbil ACx tuned to modulation detection, suggesting that juvenile and adult animals may not equivalently access the sensory information in these most sensitive neurons ( Rosen et al. 2010 ). Differential use of sensory information could amplify the age differences visible with the use of the cell-by-cell and population analyses applied in the present study, but this would need to be assessed by recording in decision-making regions during task performance.

span.label: with the developmental interpretation flagged as conditional - IF juveniles integrate over a longer window, they would experience larger dynamic range differences
span.quote: The present data show an age difference for correlation of dynamic range difference with masked signal detection only in the narrow ToneWin. However, it may not be necessary to see an age difference in dynamic range reductions to anticipate an age effect. If juveniles integrate over a longer window than adults, they would experience larger dynamic range differences due to incorporating more firing activity from the masker.

span.label: and the locus argued from where the phenomenon is and is not found - backward masking appears in the inferior colliculus but not the auditory nerve or cochlear nucleus, and cannot be peripheral because the signal precedes the masker
span.quote: The neural mechanisms contributing to temporal masking, both backward and forward, have been attributed to central auditory regions, because temporal masking functions are not sufficiently explained by responses in the auditory periphery ( Plack and Oxenham 1998 ; Relkin and Turner 1988 ). Forward temporal masking, where the neural response to a tone following a masker is altered, has been described at several levels of the auditory pathway ( Brosch and Schreiner 1997 ; Calford and Semple 1995 ; Ingham et al. 2016 ; Nelson et al. 2009 ). Forward masking effects are larger in ACx than in presynaptic regions and involve independent inhibitory mechanisms, indicating that higher level computations enhance forward masking ( Alves-Pinto et al. 2010 ; Calford and Semple 1995 ; Nelson et al. 2009 ). Individual differences and large variability, which are indicative of central contributions, are greater in backward than in forward masking ( Buss et al. 1999 ; Oxenham and Moore 1995 ). However, potential neural contributions to backward masking are unresolved. Because the signal to be detected occurs before the masker, masking cannot be fully explained by responses in the auditory periphery ( Zwicker and Fastl 2013 ). Backward masking occurs with both dichotic and monotic stimuli, also suggesting central contributions ( Elliott 1962 ). Recordings have shown forward but not backward masking in the auditory nerve ( Killian et al. 1994 ) and in cochlear nucleus neurons ( Watanabe and Simada 1971 ), but backward masking has been demonstrated in inferior colliculus ( Faure et al. 2003 ; Watanabe and Simada 1971 ). Individual differences and large variability, which are indicative of central contributions, are greater in backward than in forward masking ( Buss et al. 1999 ; Oxenham and Moore 1995 ). Because the signal to be detected occurs before the masker, masking cannot be fully explained by responses in the auditory periphery ( Zwicker and Fastl 2013 ). However, despite the involvement of cortex in temporal information processing ( Green et al. 2017 ; Ohl et al. 1999 ; Rosen et al. 2010 ), typical ACx responses to signals have never been examined during backward masking.

span.label: with variability itself taken as INDICATIVE of central contributions, being greater in backward than forward masking
span.quote: The neural mechanisms contributing to temporal masking, both backward and forward, have been attributed to central auditory regions, because temporal masking functions are not sufficiently explained by responses in the auditory periphery ( Plack and Oxenham 1998 ; Relkin and Turner 1988 ). Forward temporal masking, where the neural response to a tone following a masker is altered, has been described at several levels of the auditory pathway ( Brosch and Schreiner 1997 ; Calford and Semple 1995 ; Ingham et al. 2016 ; Nelson et al. 2009 ). Forward masking effects are larger in ACx than in presynaptic regions and involve independent inhibitory mechanisms, indicating that higher level computations enhance forward masking ( Alves-Pinto et al. 2010 ; Calford and Semple 1995 ; Nelson et al. 2009 ). Individual differences and large variability, which are indicative of central contributions, are greater in backward than in forward masking ( Buss et al. 1999 ; Oxenham and Moore 1995 ). However, potential neural contributions to backward masking are unresolved. Because the signal to be detected occurs before the masker, masking cannot be fully explained by responses in the auditory periphery ( Zwicker and Fastl 2013 ). Backward masking occurs with both dichotic and monotic stimuli, also suggesting central contributions ( Elliott 1962 ). Recordings have shown forward but not backward masking in the auditory nerve ( Killian et al. 1994 ) and in cochlear nucleus neurons ( Watanabe and Simada 1971 ), but backward masking has been demonstrated in inferior colliculus ( Faure et al. 2003 ; Watanabe and Simada 1971 ). One study examined backward masking within a subset of recorded cortical cells that exhibited a very delayed response (>150 ms after signal onset; Brosch et al. 1998 ). However, despite the involvement of cortex in temporal information processing ( Green et al. 2017 ; Ohl et al. 1999 ; Rosen et al. 2010 ), typical ACx responses to signals have never been examined during backward masking.

span.label: the area was chosen because inactivating it impairs temporal discrimination and because human imaging ties it to conscious masked detection
span.quote: ACx is important for temporal processing, because its ablation or inactivation impairs discrimination of temporally varying signals ( Elliott and Trahiotis 1972 ; Kelly et al. 1996 ; Ohl et al. 1999 ). Furthermore, human imaging during temporal masking reveals activity in primary ACx during detection of the signal, suggesting that ACx activity relates to conscious masked signal perception ( Wiegand and Gutschalk 2012 ). An additional motivation to focus on ACx is because it integrates brain stem and thalamic inputs and provides a sensory representation to downstream decoding centers

span.label: juvenile neurons showed both greater tone-firing suppression and larger threshold shifts, at single-cell and population levels
span.quote: In this study we have demonstrated that the onset responses of ACx neurons to short tones were clearly modulated by a subsequent masker. Neurometric thresholds shifted to higher tone levels in the presence of this masker. The higher thresholds seen during masking were attributable to a combination of suppressed firing to the tone and a smaller dynamic range available for detection during masking. In a developmental comparison, juvenile neurons showed both greater tone firing suppression and larger threshold shifts than adult neurons, at both single-cell and population levels. Our results are consistent with the human literature of higher backward masked thresholds extending into adolescence and demonstrate robust backward masking at the level of ACx.

span.label: A POOLING DECISION JUSTIFIED BY THE COMPOSITION OF THE SAMPLE: single and multi-units pooled BECAUSE the multi-units dominated
span.quote: Spikes were detected offline (Plexon Offline Sorter, Dallas TX), and sorted into single (SU) or multiunits (MU) on the basis of spike shape and principal component analysis. Adult neurons ( n = 42) consisted of 15 SUs and 27 MUs, whereas juvenile neurons ( n = 40) consisted of 10 SUs and 30 MUs. Because MUs dominated the data set, all SUs and MUs were pooled for analysis.

span.label: THE METHOD IS ALIGNED TO THE LITERATURE IT WILL BE COMPARED WITH: monaural delivery, to parallel the majority of psychophysical studies
span.quote: Stimuli were delivered monaurally to the right ear through an in-ear headphone speaker (Audio Technica ATH-CKS1100iS). This was chosen to parallel the majority of psychophysical backward masking studies that present stimuli monaurally.

span.label: AND THE INCLUSION RULE IS SET BY THE PERCEPT: only units responding reliably to short tones, because backward masking is reliable only for short tones
span.quote: Neurons were isolated based on their reliable, short-latency onset responses to a 200-ms tone pip used as a search stimulus. Offset-responsive neurons were rarely encountered and were not used in these analyses. The best frequency (BF) of the unit was determined with an iso-intensity function at 60 dB SPL. For the remaining data collection, neurons were presented with short tone pips (10 ms; 2-ms cosine-ramped rise/fall) at the BF of the unit, and only units that responded reliably to these short-duration tones were recorded (firing above baseline on at least 50% of trials within 50 ms of tone onset). This is because, perceptually, the phenomena of backward masking is reliable only for short-duration tones.

span.label: the masker was a 500 ms noise at 30% bandwidth centerd on each neuron's own best frequency
span.quote: To determine backward masking responsivity, Tone-Alone rate-level functions (RLF) were compared with Tone+Noise RLFs, where a 500-ms noise (5-ms cosine-ramped rise/fall) immediately followed the 10-ms tone ( Fig. 1, A , D , G ). The masking noise was 30% bandwidth, centered at the tone frequency, BF. Tone-alone RLFs were collected from stimuli presented at 0–80 dB SPL in increments of 5 dB, for 15 trials (with 1-s intertrial intervals). The Tone-Alone RLF was recorded first to visually estimate tone threshold (for this purpose, the lowest tone level with a clear increase in spiking above lower levels). Subsequently, we recorded several backward masked Tone+Noise RLFs, collected at three to four masker levels (separated by 10 dB). Masker levels were chosen to range around and above the estimated tone threshold level of the neuron. Masked RLFs included a subset of the full range of tone levels collected in the Tone-Alone RLF, chosen to include a response to noise alone (0 dB SPL tone), and a range of tone levels below and above tone threshold. All stimuli were preceded by a 50-ms period of silence to measure spontaneous activity.

span.label: this is the first assessment of backward masking in STANDARD onset-responsive cortical neurons, and both coding elements contribute
span.quote: This study is the first to assess whether backward masking of tone detection occurs at the level of primary auditory cortex for standard, onset-responsive neurons, how it manifests, and whether it mirrors the prolonged development seen in children. Backward masking is the neural “detection” of a masked signal compared with the masker alone, in contrast to signal detection compared with silence. We showed that the majority of ACx neurons displayed increased thresholds for tone detection in the presence of a subsequent masker. This was the case with the use of a narrow ToneWin that measured backward masking by minimizing contamination from the noise-evoked response, as well as a longer TrialWin that intentionally included the noise-evoked response, as a potential contributor to perceptual backward masking. This “masking” correlated with both suppression of tone-evoked firing by the masker and with the reduced dynamic range of the tone detection function in the presence of a masker. This indicates that both a reduction of signal response and a higher comparative baseline contribute to auditory backward masking.

span.label: with the two elements dissociating across development - larger suppression in juveniles but no difference in dynamic range reduction
span.quote: With this characterization, we then asked whether the extended human maturational trajectory for backward masking is reflected in ACx responses, as would be expected based on cortical involvement in conscious masked signal detection ( Wiegand and Gutschalk 2012 ). Tone threshold shifts were larger in juveniles than in adults, indicating greater cortical backward masking. This was accompanied by a larger suppression of tone-evoked firing in juveniles, but no age-related difference in dynamic range reduction, indicating that greater juvenile masking in cortex was driven more by suppressed tone-evoked firing than by increased noise-evoked baseline. However, dynamic range reduction measured in the narrow ToneWin correlated with masked tone threshold shift only in juveniles, suggesting that dynamic range may contribute more to signal detection in juveniles than in adults.

span.label: THE anesthetic IS JUSTIFIED BY MECHANISM: urethane acts modestly on several receptor systems and allows desynchronised activity closer to the awake state
span.quote: Anesthesia is one concern in extending our neural responses to psychophysical comparisons. We used anesthesia to maximize data collection during extended masking protocols; we chose urethane to minimize anesthetic effects. Ketamine primarily affects NMDA receptors, and pentobarbital enhances GABA A receptor effects. Under these drugs, the cortex operates mostly in the synchronized state. In contrast, urethane anesthesia is produced by a modest effect on multiple receptor systems ( Hara and Harris 2002 ) and allows desynchronized activity to occur spontaneously in cortex, more similar to the awake state ( Curto et al. 2009 ). In the avian analog of ACx, urethane decreases both spontaneous and evoked activity ( Capsius and Leppelsack 1996 ). Because the relationship between spontaneous and driven activity drives the neural detection measures, urethane potentially minimizes any deviation from awake recordings. Qualitatively, both juvenile and adult recordings resembled those from awake, restrained gerbils ( Rosen et al. 2010 ), although restraint is known to affect cortical responses, as well

span.label: THE VARIABILITY IS ITSELF A POINT OF CORRESPONDENCE with the psychophysics, unlike the tight relationship seen for forward masking
span.quote: First, masked thresholds are quite variable, in concurrence with psychophysical data: behaviorally, backward masking thresholds are highly variable, both within and across subjects; more threshold measures need to be gathered per participant than in forward masking to yield clear data ( Hartley et al. 2000 ; Oxenham and Moore 1995 ; also Huyck JJ, personal communication). Similarly, there was not a highly systematic relationship in our ACx data between masker level and threshold shifts, unlike the tight correlation seen with cortical and psychophysical forward masking

span.label: A CORRELATE THAT IS NOT THE CAUSE, SAID PLAINLY: suppression correlated with masking but could occur in its absence
span.quote: A response to the masker was not required to produce masking, as also seen in cortical forward masking ( Calford and Semple 1995 ). Backward masking was correlated with tone-evoked firing suppression but could occur in its absence, and thus was not the sole driver of the masking.

span.label: a shorter latency for inhibition than excitation lets the later masker suppress the earlier tone, and predicts the negative correlation observed
span.quote: Mechanistically, forward masking is considered to involve a combination of synaptic depression, afterhyperpolarization, and inhibition ( Brosch and Schreiner 1997 ; Wehr and Zador 2005 ). A study of forward and backward masking in the bat inferior colliculus indicates that mechanisms involving the relative timing of inhibition and excitation at the level of the inferior colliculus can explain both types of masking ( Faure et al. 2003 ). Backward masking was attributable to fast inhibition, where a shorter latency for inhibition compared with excitation allowed inhibition evoked by the delayed masker to suppress the response to the earlier tone. Such a mechanism could explain the negative correlation seen in the present study between forward masking of the noise with backward masking of the tone in the narrow ToneWin: a suppressed response to the masker would be less effective at suppressing the tone response.

span.label: so the cortical effect may be inherited from earlier regions, with cortex possibly magnifying it
span.quote: Cortical masked responses, expressed as a reduction in tone-evoked firing, may thus be inherited from earlier brain regions. It remains possible that cortex further increases masking. In gerbil ACx, both tone-evoked afterhyperpolarizations and rebound firing were reduced in magnitude by a temporally overlapping masker ( Gay et al. 2014 ). Backward masking may induce a similar reduction of rebound excitation, which would magnify the suppression of tone-evoked firing at the level of cortex.

span.label: the backgrounds were chosen deliberately to match how a listener's two thresholds are compared
span.quote: Our neurometric comparison used Noise-Alone-evoked firing and spontaneous firing as the backgrounds against which each threshold was determined to match perceptual measures. In psychophysical detection, listeners choose between alternatives of a masker with and without a tone, to yield a masked detection threshold. A separate choice between silence and a tone yields a Tone-Alone detection threshold. The two thresholds are then compared to yield a mask-induced threshold shift. Because the masker immediately follows the tone, a longer detection window such as the TrialWin will encompass the response to the masker, making the relative background level a critical element of detection above baseline. In contrast, only a very short analysis window will exclude the Noise-Alone-evoked firing background.

With the use of this strict analysis window, our data revealed that backward masking was visible at the level of auditory cortex, that tone detection thresholds were higher in juvenile neurons, and that tone-evoked responses were more suppressed by a backward masker in juvenile neurons. Furthermore, the dynamic range difference, a cue available for masked signal detection, only correlated with backward masking in juveniles for this narrow window, suggesting a possible differential use of dynamic range in masked signal detection across development.

span.label: THE CORRECT WINDOW CANNOT BE DETERMINED FROM THIS DATA: it would need trial-by-trial mapping of activity onto behavioral choice
span.quote: Although the ToneWin measures backward masking of the tone, it is unknown whether the nervous system is analyzing activity only within this window to decide whether a tone is present. Understanding the relationship between individual neurons’ activity and perceptual judgment requires the choosing of an analysis window that mimics the decision window used by the listener. However, this window is typically variable and difficult to determine ( Nienborg et al. 2012 ). Understanding the relevant time windows that contribute to perception requires trial-by-trial mapping of neural activity with behavioral choice

span.label: IN LIEU OF SUCH DATA the longer window is chosen for two named reasons - the comparison is against the masker alone, and the reaction time falls after masker onset
span.quote: In lieu of such data, we chose the TrialWin to encompass the response to both the tone and the masker for two reasons: 1 ) perceptually, tone detection in the presence of a masker is measured in comparison to the masker alone, and the masker response occurs immediately following or even overlapping the preceding tone response; and 2 ) the behavioral reaction time for short signal detection occurs well after subsequent masker onset, suggesting that neural responses to the masker may contribute to masked signal detection.

span.label: 18-43 dB of shift in the longer window against 13-16 dB in the narrow one, with human psychophysics at 20-35 dB
span.quote: Consistent with this idea, the TrialWin population neurometric threshold shifts (~18–43 dB in adults) are a better match to psychometric backward masking thresholds than the ToneWin shifts (~13–16 dB in adults). In humans, masking parameters similar to those used here yield threshold shifts of ~20–35 dB ( Elliott 1962 ; Pickett 1959 ). Indeed, more units exhibited higher threshold shifts with the use of the TrialWin than the ToneWin, and this was reflected in the population neurometrics. Perception of masked signals may thus rely on longer time windows, where the neural response to the masker would increase backward masked detection thresholds.

span.label: A STRENGTH AND A LIMITATION IN ONE SENTENCE, with the rival lower-envelope principle named
span.quote: A strength and limitation of the population neurometric used in the present study is that it pools information across all cells to make a decision for or against tone detection. In general, population coding assumes that all active neurons contribute to perception, whereas the lower envelope principle assumes that perception is driven by the most sensitive neurons and that less sensitive neurons will not interfere

span.label: AND THE DIRECTION OF THE OWN BIAS SPELLED OUT: testing every neuron at its own best frequency makes the pooled measure optimistic
span.quote: Because all neurons in this study were presented with stimuli at BF, our neurometric does not reflect the situation where a downstream integrator neuron would also receive input from cells that were poorly tuned to the stimulus. In studies where neurons were explicitly tested with preferred and nonpreferred stimuli, pooling of all active neurons regardless of their stimulus specificity reduced the performance of the neurometric, effectively raising detection thresholds ( Purushothaman and Bradley 2005 ). This effect held true for neurons in ACx, where neural performance for song discrimination in songbirds ( Wang et al. 2007 ) and for encoding amplitude modulation depth in gerbils ( Rosen et al. 2010 ) only achieved accuracy as good as behavior when only the best neurons were included. Thus the performance of the pooling neurometric on masked tone detection should be reduced by incorporating responses from nonresponsive neurons, but whether this effect would vary across age is unknown.

span.label: AND THE AUTHORS' OWN EARLIER NULL COMPLICATES IT: no age difference in the best neurons, so the difference may be in ACCESS rather than encoding
span.quote: In a previous study, we observed no age difference in the thresholds of the best neurons in gerbil ACx tuned to modulation detection, suggesting that juvenile and adult animals may not equivalently access the sensory information in these most sensitive neurons ( Rosen et al. 2010 ). Differential use of sensory information could amplify the age differences visible with the use of the cell-by-cell and population analyses applied in the present study, but this would need to be assessed by recording in decision-making regions during task performance.

span.label: children LISTEN LATE with respect to a signal, and may be integrating over a longer window than adults
span.quote: The closer match of the population TrialWin thresholds to psychophysical data suggests that individuals are not making decisions based solely on very brief time windows following tone onset. Accurate perception within narrow time windows is measured by temporal resolution tasks such as gap detection, or detection of short signals. Performance on temporal resolution tasks is typically immature into adolescence. Indeed, tasks designed to probe temporally selective listening indicate that children “listen late” with respect to a signal ( Hall et al. 2007 ). For example, children are not as efficient as adults at distinguishing signals closely spaced in time ( Fox et al. 2010 ) and have higher thresholds for short signals ( He et al. 2010 ), both of which may relate to their ability to process neural activity in narrow temporal windows. Thus, perceptually, children may be integrating across a longer time window than adults. This would incorporate more of the masker-induced baseline firing, which would reduce the dynamic range of comparison, and could contribute to higher backward masked thresholds seen in children.

span.label: with the developmental interpretation flagged as conditional - IF juveniles integrate longer, they WOULD see larger dynamic range differences
span.quote: The present data show an age difference for correlation of dynamic range difference with masked signal detection only in the narrow ToneWin. However, it may not be necessary to see an age difference in dynamic range reductions to anticipate an age effect. If juveniles integrate over a longer window than adults, they would experience larger dynamic range differences due to incorporating more firing activity from the masker.

span.label: and the slow maturation attributed to inhibition, which decays more slowly and summates more in young neurons
span.quote: An additional challenge to juvenile signal detection with backward maskers is the greater tone-evoked firing suppression shown in the present study. In addition to inefficient temporal integration, this differential signal suppression could contribute to the large age-related threshold differences seen in psychophysical backward masking (~25-dB differences around age 9, and still ~10-dB differences by age 15; Huyck and Wright 2018 ; Wright and Zecker 2004 ). Although the basis for backward masking is poorly understood, its gradual maturation implies that neural mechanisms with long developmental time courses may be involved ( Rosen et al. 2010 ). Inhibition in the central auditory system is known to have a long developmental trajectory ( Chang et al. 2005 ; Gao et al. 1999 ; Sun et al. 2010 ) and to sculpt responses to time-varying percepts such as frequency modulation discrimination, forward masking, and duration tuning ( Razak and Fuzessery 2007 ; 2009 ; Sayegh et al. 2014 ; Volkov and Galazyuk 1992 ; Zhang et al. 2003 ). Tone-evoked suppression via masking likely involves inhibitory circuitry. In juveniles, the differentially increased suppression in the presence of a noise masker that activates off-frequency neurons may be due to unrefined inhibition in cortex or in presynaptic regions. Immature on-frequency inhibition may also contribute. In cortical pyramidal neurons, the decay time constants for inhibition are much slower during development than in adulthood ( Cai et al. 2017 ; Takesian et al. 2012 ). Closely spaced stimuli led to greater overlap and summation of inhibition in young neurons when tested in vivo ( Cai et al. 2017 ). Thus a larger inhibitory response to the subsequent masker might differentially truncate a previous excitatory response to the tone in young neurons, magnifying tone-evoked firing rate suppression. In contrast to firing rate suppression, the masker-induced reduction in dynamic range only differs across age for the narrow ToneWin. The firing suppression may thus be a particular driver of increased backward masked thresholds in Juveniles. Overall, the slow maturation of backward masking may be influenced by the gradual development of inhibition throughout the auditory pathway.

span.quote: NEW & NOTEWORTHY In children, auditory detection of backward masked signals is immature well into adolescence, and detection deficits correlate with problems in speech processing. Our auditory cortical recordings reveal immature backward masking in adolescent animals that mirrors the prolonged development seen in children. This is driven by both signal-evoked suppression and dynamic range reduction. An extended window of analysis suggests that differences in temporally focused listening may contribute to late maturing thresholds for backward masked signals.

span.quote: With this characterization, we then asked whether the extended human maturational trajectory for backward masking is reflected in ACx responses, as would be expected based on cortical involvement in conscious masked signal detection ( Wiegand and Gutschalk 2012 ). Tone threshold shifts were larger in juveniles than in adults, indicating greater cortical backward masking. This was accompanied by a larger suppression of tone-evoked firing in juveniles, but no age-related difference in dynamic range reduction, indicating that greater juvenile masking in cortex was driven more by suppressed tone-evoked firing than by increased noise-evoked baseline. However, dynamic range reduction measured in the narrow ToneWin correlated with masked tone threshold shift only in juveniles, suggesting that dynamic range may contribute more to signal detection in juveniles than in adults.

span.label: window
span.quote: Neurometric analysis requires the choosing of an appropriate encoding time window, defined as the window containing the response patterns contributing to the signal to be detected ( Panzeri et al. 2010 ). For these neurometric analyses, we employed two windows to test different aspects of masking. First, a brief analysis window encompassed only the response to the tone without any response to the successive masker. This quantified backward masking of the tone response while excluding forward masking of the subsequent masker response by the tone, allowing a measure of cortical backward masking uncontaminated by a forward masked component. Second, a longer analysis window encompassed the response to both the tone and the subsequent masker. This was used because behaviorally, tone detection in the presence of a masker is measured in comparison to that of the masker alone, and because the behavioral reaction time for short signal detection occurs well after subsequent masker onset. Thus perception of backward masked signals could be influenced by neural responses to the masker, which are encompassed by the longer analysis window. The longer window may more accurately reflect the information used by the nervous system for masked signal detection.

span.quote: Adults ( n = 16, 8 males) ranged in age from postnatal day (P)74 to P127; juveniles ( n = 18, 8 males) ranged in age from P25 to P33.

span.quote: Finally, tone detection threshold was estimated as the lowest tone level that yielded a correct response on 65% of the comparisons ( Fig. 1, C , F , and I ).

span.quote: Consistent with this idea, the TrialWin population neurometric threshold shifts (~18–43 dB in adults) are a better match to psychometric backward masking thresholds than the ToneWin shifts (~13–16 dB in adults). In humans, masking parameters similar to those used here yield threshold shifts of ~20–35 dB ( Elliott 1962 ; Pickett 1959 ). Indeed, more units exhibited higher threshold shifts with the use of the TrialWin than the ToneWin, and this was reflected in the population neurometrics. Perception of masked signals may thus rely on longer time windows, where the neural response to the masker would increase backward masked detection thresholds.

span.label: 50% of trials — the response reliability a unit had to reach to be recorded at all, a selection set by the perceptual phenomenon rather than by the recording
span.quote: Neurons were isolated based on their reliable, short-latency onset responses to a 200-ms tone pip used as a search stimulus. Offset-responsive neurons were rarely encountered and were not used in these analyses. The best frequency (BF) of the unit was determined with an iso-intensity function at 60 dB SPL. For the remaining data collection, neurons were presented with short tone pips (10 ms; 2-ms cosine-ramped rise/fall) at the BF of the unit, and only units that responded reliably to these short-duration tones were recorded (firing above baseline on at least 50% of trials within 50 ms of tone onset). This is because, perceptually, the phenomena of backward masking is reliable only for short-duration tones.

span.label: ~25-dB — the human age difference in backward masked thresholds around age nine, still about 10 dB by fifteen
span.quote: An additional challenge to juvenile signal detection with backward maskers is the greater tone-evoked firing suppression shown in the present study. In addition to inefficient temporal integration, this differential signal suppression could contribute to the large age-related threshold differences seen in psychophysical backward masking (~25-dB differences around age 9, and still ~10-dB differences by age 15; Huyck and Wright 2018 ; Wright and Zecker 2004 ). Although the basis for backward masking is poorly understood, its gradual maturation implies that neural mechanisms with long developmental time courses may be involved ( Rosen et al. 2010 ). Inhibition in the central auditory system is known to have a long developmental trajectory ( Chang et al. 2005 ; Gao et al. 1999 ; Sun et al. 2010 ) and to sculpt responses to time-varying percepts such as frequency modulation discrimination, forward masking, and duration tuning ( Razak and Fuzessery 2007 ; 2009 ; Sayegh et al. 2014 ; Volkov and Galazyuk 1992 ; Zhang et al. 2003 ). Tone-evoked suppression via masking likely involves inhibitory circuitry. In juveniles, the differentially increased suppression in the presence of a noise masker that activates off-frequency neurons may be due to unrefined inhibition in cortex or in presynaptic regions. Immature on-frequency inhibition may also contribute. In cortical pyramidal neurons, the decay time constants for inhibition are much slower during development than in adulthood ( Cai et al. 2017 ; Takesian et al. 2012 ). Closely spaced stimuli led to greater overlap and summation of inhibition in young neurons when tested in vivo ( Cai et al. 2017 ). Thus a larger inhibitory response to the subsequent masker might differentially truncate a previous excitatory response to the tone in young neurons, magnifying tone-evoked firing rate suppression. In contrast to firing rate suppression, the masker-induced reduction in dynamic range only differs across age for the narrow ToneWin. The firing suppression may thus be a particular driver of increased backward masked thresholds in Juveniles. Overall, the slow maturation of backward masking may be influenced by the gradual development of inhibition throughout the auditory pathway.
